entries.text: notebook: updated Tally-Pip
time: 20 minutes later: Day 15, 6:18:36 PM

You keep your eyes on the dirt and let your lips move. The tune comes out of you low and rough, the way it did when Dargan hummed it over the evening fold. You take up the last two lines she left hanging, where the missing goat comes home, and you sing them to the whetstone.

Pip's pen stops. He looks at you, then up the slope, then at you again. You scowl before he can open his mouth. "My father's evening song. A man's allowed to be sentimental about his dead, clerk, so write that down."

It is a poor lie. You feel it fall flat the moment it leaves you. Pip says "Mm," in the voice of someone being polite about a bad stew, and bends over his ledger. You watch his pen write a line, strike it out, and write it again, slower. He doesn't say what it is. When he glances up, his bright eyes are troubled rather than sly, which is worse in its way. He likes the goat meat. He may not like what he is about to decide.

Up on the gate-top the last of the washing comes down. A small hooded shape gathers the cloths in her arms and pauses at the parapet for the length of one breath, facing the valley, not you. Then she is gone down the ledger-house stair.

It is just past six on day fifteen. The dusk bell has rung, and the second-wall guards are well into their flask. Five days remain before midwinter's eve. Pip is watching you, ledger shut on his thumb, waiting to see what kind of man you are.

time: 20 minutes later: Day 15, 6:18:36 PM

You keep your head down and your lips barely moving, and you hum the last two lines of the song, rough and low, where the lost goat finds the fold and comes home. Pip's pen stops. He looks at you sidelong.

"My father's evening song," you mutter, and scowl as hard as you can. "A man's allowed to be sentimental about his dead, clerk. Write that down."

After a moment, something small and pale is pegged at the end of the line, a rag knotted in a way you remember. It is a herder's tally knot, the kind a shepherd ties to say *counted, all present.* It faces the second gallery, and it hangs there in the wind.

Then the hand is gone, the line sways, and the dusk bell finishes tolling. It is a quarter past six on day fifteen. Five days remain, and she knows you heard her.

You tell him in your best bellow, pitched low for the walls, that he lives if he sits quiet. He goes limp with terror. You bind his wrists and gag him with his own sash, tight and quick, and then, because his eyes are rolling at the strongbox under the desk and he is trying to say something around the gag, you loosen it a finger's width. The order came today: the children and the master ledger go down the deep shaft at *dawn tomorrow*, and the spare key to the Tin Row is in the box. He points with his chin.

You take the key. You tie the gag tight again and leave the scribe sitting in the glow with his eyes shut.

It is twenty past ten. The fire at the east sheds is climbing, and the wall is loud with the guards. The master ledger is still unburned in the Foreman's chest at the third gate, and the children go down the shaft at dawn, not in two days. Pip lies awake in the barracks, and Gorrak's column is on the road. You have a Tin Row key in your belt and Tessa waiting at the wash-house door.

You finish your shift like any tired man and eat your porridge. At the second bell you rise again, this time with the greataxe on your back and a torch from your pack. You make no secret of it to yourself that tonight Dargan's axe goes with you. You are not quiet. A loose board answers your heel, and when you glance back, a small shape in the next bunk is a shade too still, with the cap tipped a shade too far over its eyes. Pip is only pretending to sleep.

Outside, the cold is sharp and the smelters throw their red light on the underside of the smoke. You strike the tinderbox in the lee of the east coal shed, the one farthest from the third gate's stair, and put the flame to the oil-black planks. It takes quickly. Coal dust catches, then the roof-felt, and by the time you have crossed the yard, the shed is a roaring orange lantern.

"Fire!" Someone is bawling it from the wall already. You drop into the shadow beside the Counting House and wait, the axe-haft against your cheek. The two door guards come out of the building, swearing, and one of them runs for the shed with a bucket. The other starts to follow, then stops, because you made a mistake that you realize an instant too late: the firelight is throwing your shadow, long and horned, across the slate wall at his feet.

He turns. He is a hobgoblin in chain with a shield on his arm, ten feet away, and his mouth is already opening to shout. His partner is thirty feet off and moving away, and the door to the Counting House, the lamp, the scribe and the shelf with the copy is open behind him.

You are crouched in the shadow beside the Counting House before the first shout goes up. "Fire! The sheds!" Both door guards come out at a run and pound away down the cinder slope with buckets and curses, and neither looks your way.

input.add_to_description: Day 19 ~3:10 PM: column marched six hours up the high road toward Harrowmere. Tessa scouted ahead and returned: a hobgoblin column (about twenty, tin-masked captain at its head with a rod, Sergeant Ushk beside him) is coming down the road two miles ahead, marching, not running, with a narrow stone bridge and an old drovers' fold between. The Foreman's scouts still shadow from the ridge.

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger

You get them up. Ninety-four children rise out of the grass in ragged stages, and the smallest ride on bigger backs or on yours, a girl of four with her fists wound in your sash. You cross the stream at the shallows and take the high road south, shield on your arm, with the breath banked in your chest.

Tessa goes ahead hooded and quick, a rust-colored shadow slipping along the verge, and is gone in minutes. The march is slow and quiet. Ninna keeps the count at every bend. By noon the children are dragging; you stop twice to drink. The grey shape on the ridge follows, always the same distance behind.

It is a little after three in the afternoon when Tessa comes back, running low. "Twenty, maybe more," she says, breathless, in Draconic. "Hobgoblins on the road, two miles on. Marching, not running. Tin mask at the head with a rod, and a big sergeant beside him with no helm, Ushk. There's an old drovers' fold on the left and a narrow stone bridge past it. They'll reach the bridge before we do, if we keep on." She wipes her face. "They haven't seen me. I don't think they've seen us at all."

The column behind you is strung out for a quarter mile along the road, children slumped and silent. You have 5 hit points, a longsword, a shield, a breath weapon, and your sister watching your face. The fold would hold the children out of the road. The bridge is the only crossing for miles.

input.add_to_description: Day 19 ~5:10 PM: Vael was already marching north on the high road to reach Greyshaft's gate by midwinter's eve (Day 20), as he ordered Korvash to do; his column (about twenty hobgoblins, Sergeant Ushk beside him) met Tessa's scouting on the road and is about half a mile south of the stream-crossing column, closing at a march. Tessa has hidden the children in a dry wash off the road.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gorrak Vael

You get the column on its feet, and it moves. The littlest ride on bigger backs, Ninna keeps the count at every rest, and you walk the rear with the shield on your arm and the grey scouts always a long way behind. Tessa goes ahead along the high road, hooded and quick. The day wears down mile by mile. You carry two children in turn, drink at every brook, and the road stays empty.

It is a little after five in the evening, with the light going long and amber, when she comes back at a run. She doesn't slow until she's at your elbow, and she speaks low and fast in Draconic.

"Column on the road. South, maybe half a mile, and coming up at a march. Twenty or so, in the Tallies' grey. A tin mask at the head, and the sergeant with the ring in his ear beside him." She means Ushk, you think, though she doesn't know the name. "They haven't seen us. They're going to Greyshaft, Kor. He said midwinter's eve, remember? They're not hunting us. They're keeping your appointment."

She has already tucked the children into a dry wash below the road, out of sight, with Ninna in charge. The grey scouts on the ridge behind are still there. Gorrak Vael's column will pass the head of the wash in a few minutes, on the open road.

You are at 5 hit points, your breath is ready, and Rage is spent. You have a longsword, a shield, and a ring of keys. You swore Gorrak a year and a day, and you have just broken the spirit of it. What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 19 ~noon: marching up the high road from Cinder Ford with about thirty Tallies, toward the column of freed children; will meet them within the hour.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gorrak Vael

You get the column up and across the stream. Boys wade it holding smaller sisters, and Ninna counts them over twice. Then you take the high road at the rear with the shield on your arm and your breath banked in your chest. Tessa goes ahead, hooded and quick, and is soon only a rust-colored flicker among the roadside rocks.

The morning wears on. The road climbs and bends, and the children walk in their silent chain. Twice you carry someone for a mile, and your side aches the whole way. The grey scouts stay on the ridge behind, always the same distance back.

A little past noon Tessa comes down off a boulder and falls in beside you without a sound. "They're coming," she says, low. "Thirty hobgoblins, maybe more, marching in column. A tin mask at the head, with a rod in his belt. They're two miles ahead at the bend where the road meets the ford, and they're moving fast. He's earlier than the scouts said." She wets her lips. "They haven't seen us. We have maybe half an hour before they round the bend."

The road here runs through a shallow dell with scree on one side and a dry stone wall on the other, open enough that nobody can be ambushed and nowhere for ninety-four children to hide. The grey shape on the ridge behind has crept a little closer.

It is noon, you have 5 hit points and your breath weapon, and Vael is half an hour off. What does Korvash do?
